Artificial intelligence / Essay 002

Agents need taste, not more tools

Capability is abundant. Judgment is the new scarce resource—and the hardest one to benchmark.

By The EditorsOctober 3, 2026 · 6 minute read
∞
Filed under
AI / Craft

Give an agent enough tools and it can produce almost anything. That is exactly the problem. When possibility becomes cheap, selection becomes valuable.

The next frontier is not another connector or a longer context window. It is the ability to distinguish a merely valid answer from a fitting one—to recognize when the work is technically complete but spiritually unfinished.

Taste is compressed experience

Taste is often mistaken for preference. It is closer to a model of quality built from thousands of comparisons: the sentence that lands, the abstraction that leaks, the detail that makes a product feel inevitable.

An agent that can do everything still needs a reason to choose this.

We know how to test whether a system completed a task. We are much worse at testing whether it chose the right task, stopped at the right moment, or preserved the useful rough edge.

The benchmark after benchmarks

Good judgment is contextual, but not mystical. It can be made visible through examples, critique, constraints, and iteration. The teams building excellent agents will treat taste as infrastructure: explicit enough to transmit, alive enough to evolve.

Tools multiply output. Taste compounds attention. The winners will need both.

Maniacal note № 02

Automation without judgment is just faster entropy.
